tier_reason: docs/benchmarks.md compares rsloop directly with uvloop 0.22.1 (plus stdlib asyncio and zuvloop) using public harnesses benches/compare_event_loops.py and benches/workload_matrix.py, and names the CPU (Intel Core i9-9900K), kernel and CPython 3.14.7. At the benchmark commits (5d0a2bb, 6cc3444) the repo pins rustc 1.98.1 (rust-toolchain.toml) and the release profile (opt-level=3, lto="fat", codegen-units=1) that `maturin develop --release` uses, so compiler, flags, CPU and code are all available (same standard as the xutf precedent).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.98.1 (pinned in rust-toolchain.toml at bench commits 5d0a2bb/6cc3444); Cargo [profile.release] opt-level=3, lto="fat", codegen-units=1, incremental=false; built with `maturin develop --release`; CPython 3.14.7; uvloop 0.22.1; zuvloop 0.0.16 (microbenchmarks) / 0.0.14 (workload matrix)
corrections.claimed_speedup: 5,000 TCP roundtrips (Sept 14 2026, rsloop 0.1.52): rsloop 83.30 ms vs uvloop 127.87 ms (~1.53x, derived from page data); rsloop also edges uvloop on 200,000 callbacks (47.77 vs 52.67 ms) and 50,000 tasks (88.29 vs 92.85 ms), but zuvloop is fastest on those two. Sustained matrix (Sept 7 2026, rsloop 0.1.49, 16 connections): TLS HTTP 72,496 vs 26,226 ops/s (~2.76x), bulk transfer 2,009.9 vs 1,264.9 MiB/s (~1.59x), mixed streams 43,795 vs 34,196 (derived from page data); uvloop beats rsloop on plaintext `websockets` (25,800 vs 24,667), aiohttp WebSocket (32,765 vs 31,636), Starlette WebSocket (20,407 vs 18,785) and marginally raw WebSocket (4,890 vs 4,870), and zuvloop leads plaintext HTTP keep-alive. Idle activation first-reply median 17.221 ms vs uvloop 18.193 ms, but the page rates the paired p95 comparison (-23.5%, 95% interval [-48.6%, +5.9%]) as inconclusive.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark (same author wrote rsloop and the harness) but careful: pinned dependency versions, medians of 7 runs after 2 warmups in fresh subprocesses, confidence intervals for idle latency. The TCP-roundtrip win uses rsloop's native fast streams while the other loops use stdlib asyncio streams (`--no-rsloop-fast-streams` gives the like-for-like run, not published). Microbenchmarks and the workload matrix come from different runs and rsloop versions (0.1.52 vs 0.1.49) with unrestricted CPU affinity and other host services running. rustc version and release flags come from the repo (rust-toolchain.toml, Cargo.toml), not from the benchmarks page. Idle-latency advantage is labelled inconclusive by the author.

notes: All claimed numbers appear on docs/benchmarks.md. The record wrongly said uvloop beats rsloop on callbacks and tasks; on the Linux run only zuvloop does. Default branch master was last committed 2026-09-15; the 2026-09-25 date is a push to side branch perf/nightly-allocator-api. Stars 203, Apache-2.0, not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: The README table compares BusterMQ with Go nats-server on an AMD 9950X, and the harness is public (benchmark_pubsub.sh driving examples/benchmarks/bench_pub_sub.zig and bench_pub_sub_route.zig). The repo pins Zig 0.15.2 (MODULE.bazel) and release_fast/opt (.bazelrc), but the README states no compiler or flags and the nats-server version is never given, so it is first-party partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Like-for-like standard NATS protocol (same bench_pub_sub client): BusterMQ 2.98M msg/s publish, 28.86M delivery, 4.03 GB/s, p50 11.43 ms, p99 92.55 ms vs Go NATS 2.16M, 21.09M, 2.94 GB/s, p50 55.70 ms, p99 104.00 ms (~1.38x publish rate, ~1.37x bandwidth, ~4.9x lower p50; derived from page data). With BusterMQ's non-standard +ROUTE shard-aware extension (different client, bench_pub_sub_route): 6.78M msg/s, 8.80 GB/s, p50 5.02 ms (~3.1x publish rate, ~3.0x bandwidth, ~11x lower p50 vs Go NATS; derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Pub/sub fan-out benchmark from benchmark_pubsub.sh: 10 publishers, 10 subscribers, 10 topics, 50M messages of 128 bytes (~10x fan-out), server pinned to cores 0-15 with 16 benchmark client threads; BusterMQ run in Standard, Std+BusyPoll, +ROUTE and +ROUTE+BusyPoll modes; Go nats-server run at default config via taskset with the standard bench_pub_sub client
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. The repo pins Zig 0.15.2 (MODULE.bazel, rules_zig 0.12.2) and .bazelrc defaults to --compilation_mode=opt with rules_zig mode=release_fast; benchmark_pubsub.sh builds with --config=nixos. nats-server (Go) version and build not stated.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (README: '9950x'), 16 threads for the server, 16 for the benchmark client; OS/kernel not stated
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1 star; Show HN post 134 points, 65 comments (2026-01-01)
corrections.caveats: First-party, self-run, single-host, single unrepeated run. The 3x headline needs BusterMQ's +ROUTE protocol extension and a shard-aware client, while Go NATS was driven by the standard client; the standard-protocol win is ~1.38x throughput. nats-server version unstated and run at defaults. The README's Benchmarks section shows only the bench_pub_sub_route command, but the table matches benchmark_pubsub.sh output. The repo is a single commit (2026-01-01); in the HN thread the author called it a personal-rig test, 'not a nats replacement', with no time to maintain it. Homepage bustermq.sh no longer resolves. Core NATS features only (no JetStream, group queues pending).

notes: Numbers match the README exactly. Verdict is downgrade for an overstated headline (the +ROUTE mode uses a non-standard protocol extension); tier stays C. maintenance_status left 'active' by the 12-month rule (last commit 2026-01-01), but the author signalled no ongoing maintenance.

tier_reason: Author's own blog posts (benchmark4, benchmark5) give ApacheBench req/s tables against nginx 1.25.3 and others, but state no CPU model, compiler or flags, and take the best of several runs; first-party numbers with partial methodology, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: benchmark5 (Feb 2024, hinsightd 0.10.2): 102-byte index.html at ab -c 50: 124,046 vs nginx 106,615 req/s (~1.16x); at -c 1000: 75,520 vs 74,468 (~1.01x) (derived from page data). Slower on the 89.7kB jquery.js with sendfile disabled (-c 50: 23,656 vs 34,927 req/s, ~0.68x) and on dynamic gzip of jquery (-c 50: 727 vs 973 req/s). benchmark4 (Nov 2023, 0.10.1): index.html -c 50 127,296 vs 117,021 (~1.09x), essentially tied or slightly behind at -c 250 (106,621 vs 106,725); jquery.js -c 50 28,277 vs 36,029.
corrections.workload: ApacheBench (ab) concurrency sweep c=50..1000 on one 4-core machine: 102-byte index.html, 89.7kB jquery.js with sendfile disabled on all servers, and dynamic gzip of jquery.js; hinsightd 0.10.2 (io_uring, epoll fallback) vs nginx 1.25.3, lighttpd 1.4.73, Apache 2.4.58, caddy 2.7.6 (benchmark5; benchmark4 used 0.10.1, lighttpd 1.4.72, caddy 2.7.5); hinsightd, nginx and lighttpd with 4 workers; best of several runs
corrections.caveats: Author's own blog benchmark; client and server on the same 4-core machine; no CPU model, compiler or build flags stated; best-of-N runs rather than medians. The win is only on tiny-file connection handling and fades to ~1% at high concurrency; hinsightd is clearly slower than nginx on larger files and gzip. The README itself says 'almost nginx level of performance'. License conflict: readme.md says MIT but docs/LICENSE.txt contains BSD 3-Clause text (both OSI-approved). Development branch with a reduced feature set (no reverse proxy/fastcgi yet).

notes: hin10 is the multi-threaded 0.10 branch of hinsightd (hin9 is the single-threaded legacy branch). It differs from the rejected hinsightd record only on licence: a licence file exists at docs/LICENSE.txt (BSD-3-Clause text; readme says MIT). Win/loss stays mixed and it stays stale (last commit 2024-07-02). The readme and the project MT page cite benchmark5, not benchmark4, so benchmark_url was moved there.
